title: TRACER: Trajectory Risk Aggregation for Critical Episodes in Agentic Reasoning
one_liner: A method to detect when AI agents are about to fail mid-conversation by reading the whole conversation as a trajectory instead of just the last message.
lead: AI agents that use tools (like searching the web or calling functions) often fail in ways that look fine locally. An agent might write confident-sounding words but be looping, using the wrong tool, or talking past the user. This paper introduces TRACER, which reads the entire conversation history (not just the last line) to spot these hidden breakdown signals and predict failures before they happen.

paras: When an AI agent talks to a human and calls tools (functions that fetch data or perform actions), failures often hide inside long conversations. The last message looks confident, but the agent has been looping (asking the same question twice), using the wrong tool, or drifting further from what the human actually asked. A naive approach is to check how confident the model sounds in each message separately, but this misses the pattern: confident messages can be part of a broken trajectory.

Existing methods measure only single-message confidence (like how sure the model is when it picks its next word). They do not see that an agent repeating the same tool call three times in a row, or oscillating between contradictory states, is already in trouble even if each message individually looks reasonable.

callout.html: Single-message confidence misses trajectory-level breakdowns like looping, incoherent tool use, or user-agent misalignment that span many turns.

steps.text: Read every message from start to finish, not just the last one.
Detect when the model is suddenly using unusual words (a signal it is confused or shifting topics).
Count how many times the same meaning appears in nearby messages (looping).
Verify that tools being called make sense for the stated goal (not contradictory).
Combine all signals and emphasize the worst moment (the tail-end outlier), not the average.

paras: TRACER shifts the evaluation window from a single message to the entire conversation trajectory. Instead of asking how confident the model sounds right now, it asks whether the sequence of all messages, all tool calls, and all state changes looks healthy or broken.
object.object: evaluation window (single message to full trajectory)

hidden.name: Trajectory risk score
paras: Trajectory risk is a single number from 0 to 100 that measures how likely the entire conversation is about to break. It is not just the model's confidence in one answer; it is a full reading of whether the path the agent is taking still makes sense.

The paper estimates trajectory risk by sampling four signals from the conversation: (1) content-aware surprisal (how unexpected are the words), (2) situational-awareness (is the agent still tracking the original goal), (3) semantic and lexical repetition (are we looping), and (4) tool-grounded coherence (do the function calls match the claimed plan). Each signal is a number. The final risk score is calculated by taking the maximum (worst-case) of these signals across the last few steps, not averaging them — because one really bad moment signals imminent failure.

heat.caption: Darker cells are higher-risk signals. Highlighted cells are what TRACER prioritizes. The tail (t-3 spike) predicts failure even when earlier steps looked fine.

reads.html: A score from 0 to 100 measuring how broken the agent's path looks right now. High score means the agent is likely about to fail.

A tail-focused risk functional that aggregates four trajectory signals (surprisal, situational awareness, semantic/lexical repetition, tool coherence) using a max-composite step risk to surface decisive anomalies.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: reading the whole path
paras: A single bad signal is often noise, but multiple coordinated signals across several steps are a real warning. When an agent is looping, it will show high semantic repetition (saying the same thing), high tool incoherence (calling the tool again even though it failed), and maybe some unusual words (surprisal spike). A single one might be a glitch; all three together is a trajectory failure pattern.

By scanning the full sequence instead of just the last message, TRACER sees the context that makes each signal matter. It also focuses on the worst moment (the tail, or maximum) rather than the average. If 19 out of 20 steps look fine but one step is extremely bad, the average would hide it. The max-composite (take the worst) surfaces exactly those anomalies that predict failure.

stages.s: Entire conversation: all messages, all tool calls, all state changes
Extract four signals from each turn: word surprise, goal alignment, repetition patterns, tool correctness
For each signal, compute a risk number at each time step
Take the maximum (worst) risk across the last few steps per signal
Combine these worst-case signals into a single trajectory risk score
High risk triggers a pause; low risk clears the agent to continue

math.words: The final trajectory risk is the maximum of four component risks, each measured across the conversation history. Take the worst-case signal (not the average), weight them, and threshold to decide whether the agent is safe.
math.equation: R_trajectory = MAX(alpha * MAX(surprisal_t, ..., surprisal_t-k), beta * MAX(repetition_t, ..., repetition_t-k), gamma * MAX(coherence-gap_t, ..., coherence-gap_t-k), delta * MAX(situational-drift_t, ..., situational-drift_t-k))
symbols: final risk score (0 to 1 or 0 to 100)
word-prediction surprise at time step t (how unexpected the words are)
semantic or lexical repetition score at step t (how much the message repeats earlier content)
mismatch between stated goal and tool calls at step t
how far the current state is from the original user request at step t
the last k steps (a lookback window, e.g., last 5 steps)
weights that control how much each signal matters
take the maximum (worst case) across the window, not the average

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Conversation at steps 1-5: agent asks user a clarifying question, calls tool-A, gets result, calls tool-A again, says nothing changed.
Repetition at step 5: 0.8 (tool-A called twice; semantic content very similar).
Coherence gap at step 5: 0.9 (user asked to fetch data once; calling same tool twice is incoherent).
Situational drift at step 5: 0.4 (still on topic but stalled).
Using weights alpha=0.2, beta=0.3, gamma=0.4, delta=0.1 (coherence matters most):
Score 0.36 out of 1.0 is moderate risk. Baseline (surprisal only) would give 0.06 (missed the problem).

math.note: By taking the max of multiple signals and weighting coherence heavily, TRACER catches tool-use failures that look locally confident.

charts.title: Baseline (single-message confidence)
charts.note: High confidence in each message masks the looping pattern. Baseline fails to predict failure.

charts.title: TRACER (trajectory risk)
charts.note: TRACER detects the pattern early (step 3) by reading tool-use coherence across the full path.

items.html: If the agent has only taken two steps, there is no history to see patterns in. A looping agent with deep repetition needs at least three identical or near-identical steps to register.

items.b: Legitimate repetition is hard to distinguish from looping.
items.html: Sometimes an agent must call the same tool twice (to refetch data, or to call it with a different setting). The paper uses semantic similarity to filter, but an agent that calls tool-A with a slight variation might be legitimately exploring, not broken.

items.b: Tool-use coherence requires knowing the original goal.
items.html: If the user changes their mind mid-conversation, or the goal is ambiguous, measuring coherence-gap becomes noisy. The paper assumes a stable goal; it may miss graceful pivots.

TRACER is a heuristic for when to pause the agent and ask the user for input, not a hard cutoff. An agent with high trajectory risk should ask the user to confirm the next action instead of proceeding blindly.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple conversation simulator where a user asks an agent to fetch data (e.g., retrieve a paper, then summarize it, then extract a figure). Introduce three failure modes: (1) the agent loops by calling the same tool twice; (2) the agent uses the wrong tool (calls search instead of fetch); (3) the agent drifts (starts answering a different question). Run each scenario and measure whether TRACER assigns high trajectory risk to looping and wrong-tool cases (true positives) and low risk to normal conversations (true negatives).
demo.metric_eq: AUROC = area under the receiver operating characteristic curve; plot trajectory-risk score (x-axis) against failure-or-not (y-axis); TRACER should reach 80%+ AUROC on distinguishing healthy from broken trajectories
demo.closing: The key observation: trajectory risk must spike at the moment of breakdown or just before (steps 2-3 of a 5-step conversation), while single-message confidence remains high throughout. This difference is impossible to miss if the demo runs the same conversations through both methods side by side.
